title: Networking
objectives: Map the OSI model onto TCP/IP

sections.markdown: Networking connects devices so they exchange data using agreed protocols organized in layers (the OSI and TCP/IP models).

Sending a **letter**: you write it (Application), put it in an addressed envelope (Transport/Network), trucks route it (Network), and roads/planes carry it (Physical). Each layer only cares about its own job.

sections.code:
Encapsulation (going down the stack):
  data:                 [ HTTP body ]
  +TCP header:     [TCP][ HTTP body ]
  +IP header:  [IP][TCP][ HTTP body ]
  +Ethernet:  [ETH][IP][TCP][data][CRC]

sections.markdown:
## Addressing
- **IP address**: logical host address (IPv4 32-bit, IPv6 128-bit).
- **MAC address**: hardware address used within one link.
- **Port**: identifies a process/service (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443).
- **Socket**: the (IP, port) endpoint of a connection.
A connection is uniquely identified by its **5-tuple**: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, and protocol.

flashcards.front: Difference between IP and MAC address?
flashcards.back: IP is a logical, routable host address; MAC is a hardware address used within a single link.
The endpoint of a connection — the pair (IP address, port).
Each layer wraps the data with its own header going down, and strips it going up.

quiz.q: Which uniquely identifies a TCP connection?
quiz.explain: Connections are tracked by the full 5-tuple.

quiz.q: At which layer does IP operate?
quiz.explain: IP is the Internet/Network layer protocol responsible for routing across networks.

options: A specific process/service on a host
quiz.explain: Ports let one host run many services (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, etc.).
